claim: The proportional recovery rule (PRR) posits that most stroke survivors can expect to reduce a fixed proportion of their motor impairment.
source: The proportional recovery rule (PRR) posits that most stroke survivors can expect to reduce a fixed proportion of their motor impairment.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the PRR presented in the abstract, representing the authors' characterization of the model.

claim: Patients with worse motor impairment in the immediate post-stroke period will typically see the largest absolute reductions in impairment during the first 3–6 months of recovery.
source: Intuition, experience, and data suggest that patients with worse motor impairment in the immediate post-stroke period will also typically see the largest absolute reductions in impairment during the first 3–6 months of recovery.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to intuition, experience, and data, though specific data is not provided in this statement.

claim: The PRR was developed through investigation of upper-extremity Fugl-Meyer assessments (FMA-UE) at baseline and at subsequent follow-up visits.
source: The proportional recovery rule (PRR) was an early attempt to describe the relationship between initial impairment and recovery through the investigation of upper-extremity Fugl-Meyer assessments (FMA-UE) at baseline and at subsequent follow-up visits, with recovery defined as the change over time (Prabhakaran et al., 2008; Krakauer and Marshall, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Prabhakaran et al., 2008 and Krakauer and Marshall, 2015.

claim: On average, a large subset of patients recovered roughly 70% of the maximal potential recovery from impairment.
source: This work indicated that, on average, a large subset of patients recovered roughly 70% of the maximal potential recovery from impairment, but a biologically distinct and smaller subgroup recovered much less ('non-recoverers').
evidence: The claim is based on prior work referenced in the context of the PRR development.

claim: A biologically distinct and smaller subgroup of patients recovered much less than the average ('non-recoverers').
source: This work indicated that, on average, a large subset of patients recovered roughly 70% of the maximal potential recovery from impairment, but a biologically distinct and smaller subgroup recovered much less ('non-recoverers').
evidence: The claim is based on prior work referenced in the context of the PRR development.

claim: The PRR has been applied across several neurological domains since its introduction.
source: Since its introduction, the PRR has been applied across several neurological domains, implemented in various ways across studies, and evaluated using several different statistical metrics (Lazar et al., 2010; Winters et al., 2015; Winters et al., 2017; Veerbeek et al., 2018; Byblow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting applications of the PRR.

claim: The PRR was reestablished as a regression model for describing recovery from upper limb impairment in Kundert et al., 2019.
source: In a recent article, we sought to reestablish the original conceptualization of the PRR as a regression model for describing of recovery from upper limb impairment (Kundert et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kundert et al., 2019.

claim: There are concerns about mathematical coupling from inclusion of the baseline value in the change score when relating change as an outcome to baseline value.
source: The concern hinges on statistical questions about the relationship between baseline values and change scores – a relationship that is often fraught, counterintuitive, and has confounded researchers and statisticians for decades (Oldham, 1962; Gill et al., 1985; Tu, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to statistical literature spanning decades.

claim: Hope et al., 2018 raised questions about the usefulness of correlations in the case of mathematical coupling.
source: Specifically, there are questions about the usefulness of correlations in the case when there is mathematical coupling from inclusion of the baseline value in the change score, the distinction between population-level descriptions and patient-level predictions; the usefulness of the PRR in functional domains other than upper-extremity motor control; the identification of 'non-recoverers', both prospectively and retrospectively; and the possibility that ceiling effects exaggerate associations or introduce non-linearity not accounted for by the PRR (Hope et al., 2018; Hawe et al., 2018; Bonkhoff et al., 2020; Bowman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hope et al., 2018 and other papers.

claim: Ceiling effects may exaggerate associations or introduce non-linearity not accounted for by the PRR.
source: Specifically, there are questions about the usefulness of correlations in the case when there is mathematical coupling from inclusion of the baseline value in the change score, the distinction between population-level descriptions and patient-level predictions; the usefulness of the PRR in functional domains other than upper-extremity motor control; the identification of 'non-recoverers', both prospectively and retrospectively; and the possibility that ceiling effects exaggerate associations or introduce non-linearity not accounted for by the PRR (Hope et al., 2018; Hawe et al., 2018; Bonkhoff et al., 2020; Bowman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple papers raising this concern.

claim: Traditional hypothesis tests focusing on 0 as a null value are inappropriate for investigations of recovery.
source: By itself, this suggests that usual tests for the significance of a correlation in which the null value is assumed to be 0 are inappropriate for investigations of recovery.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mathematical relationship between cor(x,δ), cor(x,y), and k.

claim: The correlation cor(x+y, x-y) is zero in the canonical example of mathematical coupling.
source: This correlation is zero, rather than −0.71, in the canonical example of mathematical coupling.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of Oldham's method.

claim: Oldham's method guards against false conclusions due to mathematical coupling and regression to the mean due to measurement error.
source: Thus, Oldham's method often guards against false conclusions due to mathematical coupling and regression to the mean due to measurement error.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of Oldham's method based on its mathematical characteristics.

claim: Oldham's method does not address the possibility of ceiling effects.
source: For instance, as noted by both (Hope et al., 2018 and Hawe et al., 2018), Oldham's method does not address the possibility of ceiling effects; in our view, determining which process gives rise to observed correlations comes after assessing whether those correlations are artifacts driven by coupling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hope et al., 2018 and Hawe et al., 2018.

claim: For Dataset C200, the intercept-only, exponential, and additive models are the best performers in cross-validation.
source: For Dataset C200, the intercept-only, exponential, and additive models are the best performers; the PRR suffers from the lack of an intercept, which produces a bias in the predictions, while constant recovery with a ceiling is not well suited to this mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For Dataset D200, the PRR, exponential, and additive models are similar in cross-validation performance.
source: For Dataset D200, the intercept-only and constant recovery models are the worst performers, while the (true) PRR, exponential, and additive models are similar.
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: For Dataset E200, the constant recovery model performs best in cross-validation.
source: Finally, for Dataset E200, the (true) constant recovery model performs best.
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Cross-validation can effectively identify a best or worst model for prediction accuracy.
source: These results suggest that CV can effectively identify a best (or worst) model for prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-validation results on generated datasets.

claim: For the Stinear and Byblow dataset, k = 0.39 [0.27, 0.54] and cor(x,y) = 0.73 [0.66, 0.79].
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 1 with confidence intervals obtained through bootstrap procedure.

claim: For the Winters dataset, k = 0.07 [0.05, 0.09] and cor(x,y) = 0.59 [0.49, 0.69].
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 1 with confidence intervals obtained through bootstrap procedure.

claim: For the Zarahn dataset, k = 0.13 [0.03, 0.24] and cor(x,y) = 0.75 [0.55, 0.92].
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 1 with confidence intervals obtained through bootstrap procedure.

claim: For the real datasets, constant recovery with a ceiling underperforms against competing methods in cross-validation.
source: In these examples, constant recovery with a ceiling underperforms against competing methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The PRR appears superior for the Stinear and Byblow and Zarahn datasets in terms of prediction accuracy.
source: The exponential model, additive model, and PRR prediction accuracies are often comparable, although the PRR appears superior for the Stinear and Byblow and Zarahn datasets.
evidence: The claim is supported by the cross-validation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The PRR explains 55% of outcome variation for the Stinear and Byblow dataset.
source: Stinear and Byblow	0.55
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 2.

claim: The PRR explains 35% of outcome variation for the Winters dataset.
source: Winters	0.35
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 2.

claim: The PRR explains 56% of outcome variation for the Zarahn dataset.
source: Zarahn	0.56
evidence: The claim is directly stated in Table 2.

claim: Data among recoverers is consistent with the PRR for each study examined.
source: The preceding results suggest that data among recoverers is consistent with the PRR for each study.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bootstrap and cross-validation analyses of the three real datasets.

claim: The strong correlations between baseline and follow-up are not driven by canonical forms of mathematical coupling or regression to the mean.
source: The strong correlations between baseline and follow-up are not driven by canonical forms of mathematical coupling or regression to the mean.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bootstrap analyses showing k differs from 1 and cor(x,y) differs from 0.

claim: Competing models for recovery allowing for non-linear association between baseline and follow-up do not produce more accurate predictions than the PRR.
source: Competing models for recovery, specifically those allowing for non-linear association between baseline and follow-up, do not produce more accurate predictions than the PRR, and are similar in their fitted values.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-validation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Prior studies support the existence of a biologically distinct group of non-recoverers in upper limb motor control and deficits in other domains.
source: This assumption is supported by prior studies of upper limb motor control and deficits in other domains (Prabhakaran et al., 2008; Byblow et al., 2015; Winters et al., 2016; Zandvliet et al., 2020), and promising work suggests that it is possible to identify non-recoverers using baseline characteristics (Byblow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: It is possible to identify non-recoverers using baseline characteristics.
source: This assumption is supported by prior studies of upper limb motor control and deficits in other domains (Prabhakaran et al., 2008; Byblow et al., 2015; Winters et al., 2016; Zandvliet et al., 2020), and promising work suggests that it is possible to identify non-recoverers using baseline characteristics (Byblow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Byblow et al., 2015.

claim: Clustering methods have several weaknesses in the context of recovery.
source: Clustering refers to a collection of methods for unsupervised learning that has several weaknesses in the context of recovery.
evidence: This is a general statement about clustering methods in the context of recovery analysis.

claim: Determining the 'true' number of clusters present is imprecise and open to interpretation.
source: Perhaps more critically, determining the 'true' number of clusters present is imprecise and open to interpretation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of clustering methods based on statistical knowledge.

claim: The null hypothesis of random recovery is rejected for the Winters dataset (p<0.001).
source: Given the contrast between panels in Figure 7, it is not surprising that this approach rejects the null of random recovery for these data (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by the hypothesis test result and visual comparison in Figure 7.

claim: An inappropriate application of unsupervised learning that presumes two clusters exist can produce misleading results.
source: From this, we conclude that an inappropriate application of unsupervised learning (i.e. one that presumes two clusters exists) can produce misleading results.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of random recovery and clustering.

claim: The ability to produce slopes like the PRR through analyses of generated data does not refute the PRR.
source: Simulations of random recovery, like those in Hawe et al., 2018, and Lohse et al., 2021, are useful for illustrating these issues but should not be misinterpreted: the ability to produce slopes like the PRR through analyses of generated data does not refute the PRR (or any other model of recovery).
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of simulation studies.

claim: In many studies of upper limb motor control recovery, a distinct group of non-recoverers is clear from a visualization of the data.
source: In many studies of upper limb motor control recovery, a distinct group of non-recoverers is clear from a visualization of the data (and supported through appropriate hypothesis tests) or can be identified through a distinct biomarker, and does not artifactually arise through clustering.
evidence: This is a general statement about the observability of non-recoverers in real data.

claim: Zarahn et al., 2011 classified patients with baseline FM ≤ 10 as severely affected.
source: Zarahn et al., 2011, for example, used a subjective approach to classify patients with baseline FM ≤ 10 as severely affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zarahn et al., 2011.

claim: Bonkhoff et al., 2022 used Bayesian hierarchical models and formal model selection approaches to identify a threshold (FM = 10) above and below which patients exhibit different recovery patterns.
source: More recently, Bonkhoff et al., 2022, used Bayesian hierarchical models and formal model selection approaches to identify a threshold (also found to be FM = 10) above and below which patients exhibit different recovery patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bonkhoff et al., 2022.

claim: The severely affected population contains biologically meaningful subgroups – recoverers and non-recoverers.
source: Our point in this section, meanwhile, is that the severely affected population contains biologically meaningful subgroups – recoverers and non-recoverers – and that these can be identified using appropriate unsupervised learning methods.
evidence: This is an assertion by the authors based on their analysis and interpretation of the data.

claim: The association between initial impairment and change is non-artifactual in the examined datasets.
source: Our findings in these datasets suggest that the association between initial impairment and change is non-artifactual, and the PRR is better as a biological and predictive model than several competing models, including constant recovery with a ceiling effect.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the analyses of the three real datasets.

claim: The PRR is better as a biological and predictive model than several competing models, including constant recovery with a ceiling effect.
source: Our findings in these datasets suggest that the association between initial impairment and change is non-artifactual, and the PRR is better as a biological and predictive model than several competing models, including constant recovery with a ceiling effect.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the cross-validation analyses of the three real datasets.

claim: A biologically distinct group of non-recoverers exists.
source: These data also suggest that a biologically distinct group of non-recoverers exists.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analyses and visualizations of the real datasets.

claim: Lee et al., 2021 observed that more than half of all patients, and more than 60% of patients with baseline FMA-UE above 46, recover to the maximum possible value.
source: Lee et al., 2021, use a logistic regression to model the probability of achieving full recovery; they observe that more than half of all patients, and more than 60% of patients with baseline FMA-UE above 46, recover to the maximum possible value.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2021.

claim: The FMA-UE lacks resolution, especially at higher values.
source: Certainly, the FMA-UE lacks resolution, especially at higher values, and a refined outcome measure that ameliorates such ceiling effects is needed.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the FMA-UE measurement scale.

claim: The cohort in Lee et al., 2021 is much more mildly impaired at baseline than data observed in the current study.
source: The cohort in Lee et al., 2021, is much more mildly impaired at baseline than data we have observed; this could have several causes, but the choice to exclude patients with FMA-UE hand subscore of 0 at day 7 likely removes many moderate and severely affected patients who are unlikely to recover to ceiling.
evidence: This is an inference about the characteristics of the Lee et al., 2021 cohort based on their exclusion criteria.

claim: The PRR provides an appealingly simple model for understanding recovery.
source: The PRR provides an appealingly simple model for understanding recovery, even if the statistical approaches for evaluating it are not direct.
evidence: This is a characterization of the PRR by the authors.

claim: The PRR is and will continue to be relevant as a model for recovery.
source: We argue that the PRR is and will continue to be relevant as a model for recovery, but we agree with others that more complex analytic strategies are necessary to move beyond it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors based on their analyses.

claim: Recovery depends on factors other than initial impairment.
source: Recovery depends on factors other than initial impairment.
evidence: This is a general statement about recovery mechanisms.

claim: The PRR estimates an average recovery proportion, but individuals will recover more or less than that average.
source: The PRR estimates an average recovery proportion, but individuals will recover more or less than that average; determining whether this is 'noise' or heterogeneity that can be predicted using other forms of measure at baseline is an important next step.
evidence: This is a characterization of the PRR and its limitations.

claim: Mixed models that include both random intercepts and random slopes will have correlated random effects when applied to datasets with baseline and follow-up measurements.
source: Consider a model for outcome values at baseline (time = 0) and a single follow-up (time = 1) that includes both random intercepts and random slopes. When such a model is applied to Datasets A, C, and D, the random intercepts and slopes will be correlated; low random intercepts will suggest steeper random slopes in a way that mimics baseline and change scores.
evidence: This is an inference about the behavior of mixed models based on statistical theory.

claim: Non-linear mixed models fit to serial measurements do not avoid the challenges of mathematical coupling and changing variances over time.
source: Nonetheless, non-linear mixed models fit to serial measurements are not a panacea, and do not avoid the challenges described in this paper. The same fundamental issues that arise from within-subject correlation and changing variances over time due to recovery and measurement ceilings should be considered when using this or any other model framework.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of mixed models in the context of recovery analysis.

claim: Bonkhoff et al., 2020 found that the PRR was among the best performing models in terms of out-of-sample prediction accuracy.
source: Bonkhoff et al., 2020, fit several models to a subset of patients selected to mitigate ceiling effects and avoid including non-recoverers, and found that that PRR was among the best performing models in terms of out-of-sample prediction accuracy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bonkhoff et al., 2020.

claim: The percent of outcome variation explained by the PRR was lower in Bonkhoff et al., 2020 than in the current analyses (21% versus 35–56%).
source: The percent of outcome variation explained was lower in their work than in our analyses (21% versus 35–56%), leading the authors to suggest that the PRR may be better than other models but insufficient for making clinical predictions in the context of precision neurology.
evidence: The claim compares results from Bonkhoff et al., 2020 to the current study's results in Table 2.

claim: Bonkhoff et al., 2020 and Bonkhoff et al., 2022 use a statistically rigorous model selection approach based on leave-one-out cross-validated deviances.
source: Bonkhoff et al., 2020, and Bonkhoff et al., 2022, use a statistically rigorous model selection approach based on leave-one-out cross-validated deviances, which is particularly well suited to comparing Bayesian hierarchical models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonkhoff et al., 2020 and Bonkhoff et al., 2022.

claim: Bonkhoff et al., 2020 and Bonkhoff et al., 2022 consider only patients with initial impairments below 45 to avoid ceiling effects.
source: These papers also consider only patients with initial impairments below 45 to avoid ceiling effects induced by mildly affected stroke patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bonkhoff et al., 2020 and Bonkhoff et al., 2022.

claim: The PRR is intended as a model for recovery from a specific form of impairment as measured by the FM.
source: In light of this, we stress again that the PRR is intended as a model for recovery from a specific form of impairment as measured by the FM, and is best understood as an attempt to mathematically capture a component of the recovery process.
evidence: This is a characterization of the intended scope of the PRR.

claim: The emphasis on change between baseline and follow-up in the PRR is deliberate.
source: The emphasis on change between baseline and follow-up is deliberate: biological recovery is a process that causes a change, which then leads to the final value.
evidence: This is an explanation of the conceptual basis for the PRR.

claim: Applications of the PRR in studies of upper limb motor control recovery have often found that, averaging across recoverers, roughly 70% of lost function is regained in the time shortly after stroke.
source: Applications of the PRR in studies of upper limb motor control recovery have often found that, averaging across recoverers, roughly 70% of lost function is regained in the time shortly after stroke.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies applying the PRR.

claim: The 70% recovery proportion is attributable to spontaneous biological recovery.
source: We've argued that this is attributable to spontaneous biological recovery (Cramer, 2008; Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; Cassidy and Cramer, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cramer, 2008; Zeiler and Krakauer, 2013; and Cassidy and Cramer, 2017.

claim: The existence of a spontaneous biological recovery mechanism does not imply that behavioral interventions are unable to improve patient outcomes.
source: The existence of such a mechanism does not imply that behavioral interventions are unable to improve patient outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the PRR for interventions.

claim: Future clinical trials should seek to improve on the proportion of impairment reduction, reduce the proportion of non-recoverers, or induce changes that are distinct from and better than those expected under the PRR.
source: Instead, future clinical trials should seek to improve on the proportion of impairment reduction, reduce the proportion of non-recoverers, or induce changes that are distinct from (and better than) those expected under the PRR.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the authors' conclusions.

claim: The PRR remains a biologically relevant model of stroke recovery.
source: We conclude that the PRR remains a biologically relevant model of stroke recovery.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, drawn from all the analyses presented.

claim: All patients in the reported datasets received usual care according to evidence-based stroke guidelines for physical therapists, but no systematic interventions.
source: All patients received usual care according to evidence-based stroke guidelines for physical therapists, but no systematic interventions.
evidence: This is a description of the treatment received by patients in the datasets.

claim: Coverage of 95% confidence intervals using the bootstrap procedure is roughly 0.95 for moderate sample sizes.
source: Simulations evaluating this approach suggest that coverage of 95% CIs is roughly 0.95 for moderate sample sizes.
evidence: This is a result from simulations evaluating the bootstrap method.
